Triathlon development is the gradual coordination of three distinct sports under one recovery budget. A complete plan develops: (a) technical competence, (b) aerobic capacity and peripheral endurance, (c) sport-specific durability, (d) pacing and fueling skill, (e) transition competence, and (f) the ability to repeat quality work week after week. Race performance is therefore not predicted by a single laboratory metric or by total hours alone. Developmental sequence Novice / return-to-training: Establish reliable frequency, basic technique, pain-free movement, and realistic recovery. Use short sessions, easy intensity, and repeatable routines. The main objective is to become trainable. Developing / intermediate: Increase sport-specific volume gradually, add one or two structured quality sessions per week, build longer continuous efforts, and introduce controlled bricks. The main objective is to tolerate and absorb training while improving pacing.

Trained / advanced: Use more precise intensity control, individualized testing, race-specific blocks, high-quality intervals, strength maintenance, and a deliberate taper. The main objective is to convert accumulated fitness into event-specific performance without exceeding the athlete's recovery capacity. This sequence is not strictly linear. Illness, injury, major life stress, a long break, or a change in race distance can move an athlete back to an earlier emphasis. The planning rule is to progress the minimum effective dose first, then add volume or intensity only when the athlete demonstrates stable response.

Intensity distribution describes how training time or sessions are allocated across low, moderate, and high intensity. The labels are not interchangeable because studies define zones differently. A useful RAG answer must state the zone model before comparing distributions. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26578968/) [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39888556/) Three common patterns Pyramidal: Most training is low intensity, a smaller amount is moderate/tempo or threshold-adjacent, and the smallest share is high intensity. This often matches traditional base and build phases and can be practical when athletes need controlled sustained work.
